summary: The note profiles a revival of fermentation and pickling since September 2023, told through interviews with master fermenter Jonah Meyers and pickling artisan Rachel Armstrong. They explain the science, health benefits, beginner tips, cultural roots, and innovations such as unusual ingredients and cross-cultural ferments. Both see a future where these techniques thrive in fine dining and home kitchens.
one_line: Interviews with fermenter Jonah Meyers and pickler Rachel Armstrong on the revival, science, tips, culture and future of fermentation and pickling.
key_facts: Fermentation and pickling have been experiencing a revival since early September 2023, valued for health benefits and unique flavors.
Jonah Meyers is a chef and master fermenter interviewed on October 10, 2023.
Meyers defines fermentation as microorganisms like yeast and bacteria converting carbohydrates like starch and sugar into alcohol or acids, creating flavors, textures and probiotics.
Rachel Armstrong, a pickling artisan from the outskirts of the region, was interviewed on November 2, 2023.
Armstrong defines pickling as preserving food by anaerobic fermentation in brine or immersion in vinegar; it extends the shelf life of fresh produce.
Home fermenting and pickling surged after September 15, 2023, with hashtags like #HomeFermenting and #PicklingAdventures on social media.
A landmark conference on fermentation sciences was held on September 23, 2023, which drew interest to the science behind the methods.
Probiotics from fermentation can aid gut health and strengthen the immune system, according to Meyers.
Armstrong says pickled foods are high in vitamins and antioxidants, and the acidic environment can disable many harmful pathogens.
Meyers advises beginners to start small with sauerkraut or kimchi, stressing cleanliness and patience.
Armstrong says the salt-to-water ratio in brine is critical, and quality vinegar should not be skimped on.
Meyers cites miso and tempeh in Asian cuisine; Armstrong links pickles to Eastern European traditions.
By December 8, 2023, chefs were fermenting and pickling watermelon rinds and flowers, and cross-cultural ferments were an emerging trend.
